text: Despite the lack of shade, the lack of seating in the Beer Tent (it's usually pretty crowded), and the occasional mudfest should the weather be rainy, this is by far the best long weekend event of the year in Edmonton. The volunteers, the performers, the artists in the crafts tent, the board, and the audience all know it -- this is a world-class event. Yes, you have to either take the bus or ride your bike or get someone to drive you there. Yes, you have to buy your tickets on June 1st at 10am or risk not getting them. Yes, the food and water can be over-priced (so bring your own!). Yes, there's hardly any shade. The ski hill is a natural amphitheatre, the organization of the festival is top-notch, the mood/culture of those who attend is kind, responsible, kid-friendly, trustworthy, fun, and just darned wonderful. If you live in Edmonton, if you have ever lived in Edmonton, you will see many people you know at the Festival. It's like a reunion -- plus, you'll make new friends, too, if only your tarp neighbours. Tip for getting a tarp location of your choice on the weekend: show up at 7am sharp (not early!) in order to get your coloured/numbered slip of paper (which also has an artist's name) and group up with friends in order to get the largest number and most diverse group of slips so that when one of the colours/artists gets called out as the first group of 25 people who gets to line up, you or your group representative (hopefully with long legs for the speed walking - no running!) gets to line up early/close to the front of the line. Doesn't make sense? Just show up at 7am with a bunch of friends who are going. If you don't know anyone else who's going, maybe go anyhow and make friends in the corral (that's where you wait from 7am to 7:30am while the colours get handed out) and see if they'll group up with you. Don't bring your dog -- it gets crowded in the corral. You can leave after 7:30am and return anytime, so long as you have some way of contacting the long-legged person who placed your tarp. What did we do before cell phones? *smile* There's a Safeway in Bonnie Doon -- you can pick up food and beverages (in plastic containers only) there should you wish. Bring lots of sunscreen, reapply it often over all exposed skin! Wear a long-sleeved shirt, wear a hat. Bring layers to put on over your base layer in the evening, because it gets really cold. Some folks wear toques, really. Bring a book or a craft. Bring a comfy chair that isn't high -- look at the website that will give you guidelines re: how tall a chair can be. If you're part of a big family, bring a tent and set it up at the top of the hill -- there's a great culture of tent-dwellers at the Folk Fest and they all lookout for each other. Your kids can nap while you continue to watch the performances, plus there's a tonne of room (well, relatively) up there. Expect to be crowded if you prefer your tarp location to be close to the main stage. Buy at least one raffle ticket. Volunteer at least one year -- the folks who volunteer are *so* much fun, plus they get to go to the nightly parties that happen when the folk fest ends -- which is where the performers go to keep on playing ... plus, you get your meals for free and usually a pretty cool t-shirt. Bring two tarps at the approved size (see the website!) -- wrap the top one's edge under the bottom one when hammering in your tent pegs -- use it to cover your possessions to keep them safe from a sudden downpour, or yourself, should you be on the tarp. I remember a great afternoon concert by Blue Rodeo when it was raining HARD and there were about ten of us puppy piling under a tarp. Bring a flag and a ski pole -- attach the flag (or very visible object of your choice) to said ski pole -- and plant it beside your tarp. This is how you find your tarp, and what you tell your friends to look for when they're trying to find your tarp. And finally, be prepared to get really tired if you attend the whole thing. I usually take the following Monday off from work; I'm lucky to be able to do so. Have fun!

text: This newly opened store is an asset to the city of Newark and I am telling all my friends about it because I would love to see it thrive and stay in business for a long time. All the basic supermarket staples are there, the food is fresher, and the prices are equal to or lower than that at other supermarkets. There are also many of the standard Indian foods, including freshly baked indian breads in the refridgerator units, a whole isle of chutneys, pickles, and curry powders, and some spicy (and simple) snack foods like spiced chick-peas, more flavorful and healthier than most American snacks. Other random items of interest include incense, spices (very cheap), and varying-sized bags of high-quality rice. There are even Indian desserts in the freezer. Check this place out. It has quickly replaced the supermarket as my primary place to get fresh produce. Coming here will not only save you money, but can introduce you to some exciting new foods that you may not be able to buy anywhere else.

text: -PINBALL ALERT!- Overall I could give here 3 stars, but I'm curving to 4 because when it comes to Timeless old school video arcades in Philadelphia this is the only one that really still exists (and it's kind of sad to say it). For a fairly small arcade it has a fairly balanced offering of games to enjoy. They have new school games like DDR alongside old school games like Mrs. Pacman, 3D fighters like Soul Caliber alongside quirky Japanese 2D fighters (and plenty of sharks that are waiting to school noobs in VS mode for each), and a couple of shooting and racing games. They even have a pool hall towards the back and and plenty of games where you can win tickets for prizes. But most importantly they have Pinball! they only have newer one's like Family Guy, Pirates Of The Caribbean and The Simpsons (at least since I last checked). But they were all pretty well maintained at least. While it might be filled with plenty of tweenagers on certain occasions, I'll take an old school spot over somewhere like Dave & Busters any day of the week!
label: POS

text: I've been an AMA member since I was 16. Needless to say it's been a while. I've used AMA's roadside assistance on numerous occasions, from needing a tow, locking my keys in my car (done this too many times to count) and boosting, AMA has been there. They also provide drivers training. I took drivers training years ago and feel it helped me tremendously and is a must for every new driver (whether you admit it or not). We've used their travel services a few times and have been impressed with the quality of service provided. We've used AMA to book cross continent flights to B&B's on the west coast. If it wasn't for AMA I would have no idea where to start. Being an AMA member also provides you discounts on a number of entertainment options. The one we used the most is discounted movie tickets which are usually around half the cost of paying right at the theatre. You can also purchase concession packages. I use AMA's registry services as well for vehicle registration, business registration, birth certificates, NUAN searches, etc. They also provide insurance and mortgages. The Kingsway AMA has recently built a new building and am loving their bright, airy open concept. Plus my friend works there! The membership fee seems to go up every year. However, peace of mind certainly comes into play when it comes to travel and getting a few perks with your membership, like discounts, makes it OK in my eyes.

text: My roommate and I always come here as our default restaurant because, well, they have unlimited fries. I do like this place but there are a couple of complaints that I feel the need to share. Firstly, my friends and I (a group of 8 give or take 2) came here for breakfast and every single persons' eggs were disgustingly overcooked. This maybe might not be such a huge deal if everyone ordered scrambled (oh wait, it still would be), but most of us got eggs benedict, which were HORRIFYING. Truly, horrifying. The second is that they have this little bumper car like thing rotating in the center of the restaurant that you aren't allowed to touch or ride. Yea it is cute to look @ buuUuUut I WANT TO RIDE IT SO BAD (that's what she said) and I can't even IMAGINE what kids must think when they see that. When I was a kid and I wanted to do something, I would want it with my entire body. Oh it must be so torturous for them. Third, the meatloaf and loaded mashed potatoes were aigghhhtt... but not great, which is strange because I was having XXX fantasies about the taters... kinda disappointing. NOW the good. Their chicken finger things are DELICIOUS--crispy, salty breading surrounding the TENDER, SUCCULENT and JUICY chicken that can be dipped into ranch, beebeecue or honey mustard sauces (i'm sure there are more but my roomie and i stick to those three). The Kobe beef sliders. OMG. OMG. They use Hawaiian rolls and the grilled onions are all caramalizey and ... DROOOOOOOOLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLL!!!!!! The BLT's bread was good but the bread (Parmesan-crusted, grilled with butter or oil) was so crunchy that it was literally shredding the skin inside my mouth. OW but a delicious OW. This turkey sandwich I got with avocado and bacon was also REALLY good and HUGE. I could only eat half the 'wich and my fries... I couldn't even get a second order of fries!! Also, they always have $5 coupons floating around (the UCSB money book thing or in the clipper), which are SWEEEET and the ones that I used had no minimum purchase requirement Note: the "flavored" fries they have aren't really worth it or much better than their regular fries. I clearly eat here way too much. But I would like to add that though it is pretty scrumptious, it's part of a chain. So if you're visiting SB, you may wanna try something that you can only find in SB. I have no suggestions but hey, you're on yelp. -------------------------------- I wanted to add that I got the root beer float here and it was horrible. The root beer to ice cream ratio was all off. It was like ice cream with a splash of root beer which made the root beer foam out of control like the mouth of a rabies infested animal. They did add more root beer when I asked but all was lost by then... Derf's... now THAT place has some good root beer floats! --------------------------------- there are two gumball machines. a 25 cent jumbo gumball machine and a one cent teeny gumball machine. i forced my friend to get 10 of the one cent ones, which are obviously a better deal... for 25 cents you can get a LOT of small gumballs... plus what're you gonna do with all those pennies anyway? also, the machine is beaver brand... obviously my favorite brand in the entire world

text: Every time I go to Mama Palma's I regret it after. Yes, the pizza is good and creative, but the service is so rude I practically want to apologize to the waitstaff for inconveniencing them by coming to eat there. I went once with 5 other people-3 couples-when 4 of us arrive, the place was EMPTY and the staff refused to even take our name, much less give us a table while we waited five minutes for our friends. Once they seated us, they slapped down the menus, were back in 2 minutes, and 5 minutes later out came the pizzas. By the time there was one slice left on each of the three we had ordered, the staff came back and said "you going to eat that?" and proceeded to clear the pizza pans and dumped the slices onto a white plate. Mind you-the place was STILL empty. There was no "is there anything else we can get you?", the just dumped the check on the table. As we sat and talked (the whole point of dinner with friends), the staff proceeded to continue to clear the table, including our wine glasses despite still having wine left in the bottle. It was VERY clear we were being told to leave. The next, and last, time I went, it was again empty and my fiancee and I sat outside. We ordered one small, and the server said "you sure that's all you want?" we said we might order another later if we were still hungry, to which the server nastily told us "you can't order anything else after your first order." Again, the food was quickly brought, and our plates were even more quickly and rudely cleared. Bottom line: don't go! It's not even worth taking out because why patronize such a nasty place?

text: If you are looking for a spot to grab a delicious original bite to eat, and wash it down with a craft beer, this is your place. The mussels and fish tacos are also good if you are looking for something not quite as heavy. A side that you have to try if you don't want a full meal is the jalapeno cornbread. Sunday is half off pork menu items, which can be a really cheap meal. I saw someone order the pulled pork over the jalapeno cornbread, and was instantly jealous that I wasn't the one who ordered it. They are open for brunch on the weekends, with a menu that is similar to their usual menu, but adds some more brunchy items. If you are there to drink for the night, you need to get a table or seat at the bar, or you will be in the way of the severs the whole time. They have an extensive beer list and full bar, with a good selection of beers on draft. The crowd is a good reflection of the neighborhood, and is as diverse as it gets, but is still a very relaxed atmosphere. Outdoor seating when the weather permits is a decent bonus, with the ability to seat around 20 people outside. I am happy to say The Sidecar is my neighborhood bar.

text: After being disappointed with the previous Thai place I used to go to I decided to try this one out. I ordered takeout of Yellow Curry, Pad Thai, Clear Noodle Dish (Pad Woon Sen), and a appetizer sampler platter. The sampler platter was okay, but forgettable about the only thing that both my wife and I enjoyed was the spring rolls. The other items were either too greasy, too salty, or just too fried. The Pad Thai was a little mild for my taste, but I still enjoyed this immensely. Very light and tasty and I would recommend this if you do not like spicy food, but very tasty. The clear noodles or Pad Woon Sen is one of my favorite dishes, very light and very delicate. The noodles play well with the vegetables and was not overcooked at all, not easy to accomplish because this dish is easy to burn or cook until rubber. The Yellow Curry was the best, my wife commented that it was the best she had. It was the best I've had in a long time. I will definitely be trying this again. While I was there looking at the menu I was counting the number of times I would need to come back and try everything I wanted to order tonight, quite a few trips I need to make. I think I have found my new Thai Place.

text: We've been walking by Trattoria Victoria for a few years, so we decided to give it a try on Friday night. Since it is across street from Ca Dario, it seems to get overflow from there with no major wait time. We called an hour prior to arriving and were able to get a table no problem. Food is very good, I started with Asparagus and Prosciutto appetizer. Prosciutto was very fresh and abundant, although it could have used some olive oil or balsamic vinegar to give it some moisture. I then followed with Sea bass in tomatoes and olive puttenesca. It was fabulous, fish was very tender and fresh, with side of roasted potatoes and spinach. Husband had side of Penne (perfectly al dente), with Branzino fish. It was beautifully prepared with crispy outer skin and tender inside, waiter expertly filleted it at the table with a touch of olive oil and parsley! YUM! As with most Italian restaurants you should always try the "Special", regular menu items get boring after a while... Décor reminds me of many family owned Italian restaurants you find on east coast, a bit cramped and loud but charming (ask for table against the wall, otherwise you are sitting in prime traffic area). Not as nice as Ca Dario, more rustic. Interesting touch - they play old movies on two TV screens over bar (no sound). Clever touch, we caught the end of an old Carey Grant movie and most of Dean Martin as Matt Helm - two very stylized art directed movies, fun to watch! Movies ad an interesting "campy hip" tone. Next time we'll sit at bar, and enjoy film during dinner. Service was very good, wait staff very attentive and nice. Price is very reasonable, I read some of other reviews about it being expensive and am a bit baffled - come on this is Santa Barbra! Some of dishes are very affordable in $10 - $15 range. Wine list was decent although they could definitely add a few more reasonable priced wines in $20 - $40 range. Bathrooms need work. While an attempt was made to cutely decorate, both women's and men's rooms could use sprucing up. Let's not forget to restock toilet paper people!!! Otherwise a very nice experience!

text: I don't ever leave feedback on websites but I was really impressed and had a great experience here that I had to let people know. I missed my appointment because I had an important phone call with a customer so I called them after getting off the phone (and closing the sale) and they fit me in that day (Star #1). I waited maybe 10 minutes after some light paperwork. (Star #2). I was a brand new patient and I had been told by my previous dentist that I had a cavity and it would need filling. I moved out of state and found Dr. Walker was close to where I now live and had my old dentist transfer my records. The records they transferred were crap (one lousy copy of some x-rays). I told Dr. Walker I had a cavity and he couldn't see it readily as that xerox x-ray my previous dentist sent was useless and nothing appeared out of the ordinary from a quick inspection. He then said "it would make me feel better and give me sound of mind if we just did a quick x-ray to make sure...(and here's the best part)...I won't charge you for them." (Star #3 &4). So we did the x-rays and found the small cavity and filled it. They told me prior to anything how much it would cost, which was very reasonable. Also, I spent more time with the doctor than anyone else. He did the initial inspection, x-rays, and procedure, all seemingly without batting an eye-lash and it was no big deal. A great attitude and a great dentist (Star #5). The building is an older building but it maintained the charm of the Fountain Square neighborhood. Probably the reason they don't charge high or try to push un-needed dental work on you is that they aren't having to deal with paying huge overhead costs. They seem to be doing great business and I can see why. No T.V in the patient rooms but who cares. I don't go to the dentist to watch T.V. and pay extra for it. I just need a good dentist that is kind and knows what they're doing and doesn't charge me like crazy. I found the perfect one in Fountain Square. If I didn't live close to here, I would still travel here to get all my dental work done. I can't tell you how impressed I was with the overall experience. I never expected to be writing about a dentist experience but I was very pleased and have had some horrific dentist visits in the past. This is the first time I'm looking forward to a future dentist visit.

text: damn you, cafe ole and your delicious iced tea! that's where this whole mess began. we were siting outside and i was on iced tea number 2 or 3 when one of us mentioned scientology. we all chuckled, poking fun at john travolta. then one of us said it: let's yelp the church of scientology. i made some calls and before you know it six of us were on our way to get a "free stress test(tm)". people will read our reviews and laugh. we will be the talk of the town. pride is usually what leads to one's downfall and this story is no different. after walking west 12 blocks, one of us backed out and several of us started to get nervous. i reassured them, "remember, just act calm and interested. don't laugh, giggle, or act like a jerk. we're just going in to find out more about dianetics." but who was i kidding. i couldn't even keep a straight face while saying 'dianetics'. we walked in, all sweaty and clueless. a look of curiosity and bewilderment on our faces. perfect so far. we had to sign in and give out our contact information. some (read all) of us choose to use fake names, numbers, and addresses. we immediately aroused suspicion because five of us walked in at once. looked shady. whatever. we were immediately separated and some of us were taken back into a room with a few sofas and a TV. the woman pressed play on the DVD player and explained to us that we were going to watch a brief film on the concept of dianetics, the foundation of scientology. about 2 minutes into the film (read propaganda), i was taken into another room for my "free stress test(tm)". i was asked to hold two cylindrical tin rods connected to a machine. the woman conducting the test told me that she would ask me a series of questions and my answers would be measured by the counter on the machine, which would indicate whether i was nervous or calm. simple enough. then she began asking me personal questions. she asked me to reveal to her some of my greatest fears and concerns. the things in my life which brought me great dissatisfaction. memories of pain and heartache, loneliness and fear. we're now 20 minutes into the stress test. my eyes are transfixed on her cold, unwavering stare the entire time. i break from my trance and glance over at the machine. the needle is all the way to the right. this means i'm anxious. she now tells me to put the tin tubes down as she hands me a 600 page book. 'DIANETICS' it reads, in bold imposing letters. she tells me quite candidly to "buy it and read it". i look over and there are several advertisements throughout the lobby in which we are now sitting. they have the same slogan - "buy it and read it". she's looking right at me. into me. past my eyes, into my soul. she hasn't blinked in minutes. my god, can a human do that? aren't her eyes all dry by now? i can't even tell if she has pupils. can someone not have pupils? my heart is racing. my brow is moist and droplets of sweat are streaming down my cheek. i stumble over my words and can barely muster the ability to form a cohesive sentence, let alone an argument against why i shouldn't buy the book. after several stutters, i spit out, "let me think about it." without hesitation, she insists that i take the book. i revealed the problems in my life. things i've never told my closest friends i told this complete stranger. she's using that logic against me. she's well trained, probably from all the idiots like us who feign curiosity. i insist that i'd still like to think about it. she tells me that there's nothing to think about and instructs me to fill out a purchase form for the book. my shaky hand grasps the pen and i fill out the slip. at this point, my friends are all looking over her shoulder laughing at me and behind them the church's hired goons staring at all of us. so in the end, i'm the mark. i'm the sucker in the group. i later tried to justify my buying the book. after all, it's a philosophy like judaism, islam, hinduism. i've read all of those texts yet i am not a member of their faith. in fact, i've read most of dianetics years ago. i recall it being a mix of boring technical fluff and blustery new age hoopla. well, in the end it looks like karma got us all. i bought the book and my buddies, who felt bad for me, chipped in $5 each. i told them they can borrow it anytime but no one has taken me up on my offer as of yet. i feel bad for the scientologists. all the other world faiths are all just as illogical and allegorical and i have yet to learn of a belief system that does not blatantly attempt to sucker money and individuality from people. i guess it's socially acceptable to make fun of scientology because it's newer and created by an ascot-wearing second-rate sci-fi writer who took lots of drugs and went bat-shit crazy. ok, i used up my 5000 characters. xenu.

text: Went with family and friends from out of town on July 31, 2010. Convenient location in downtown Sparks in Victorian Square. The place was empty-kind of eerie. The dining room was also kind of cold, but nicely appointed with white tablecloths and other semi-formal finery. I did like the way the stairs with the old worn carpet led to the dining area though-kind of a secret hole in the wall feel-without being a hole in the wall. Louge singer was good, but I felt like I was listening to Peter Faulk in "Shark Tale." Service was good but sort of antagonistic. When asked if the kitchen had wheat free pasta for someone in our party who had a gluten allergy, the server replied, "Ha, no...this is a real Italian restaurant." I wanted to ask "so does being a real Italian restaurant mean the staff is insensitive to food allergies?" But I let the comment go. The server's attitude was pleasant enough-just overly cocky for the service provided and the venue. The pre-bussing was good, but the bus boy forgot or didn't want to replace several utensils after removing dirty ones. The food was good, but overall light on flavor. -The calamari appetizer was great. -The seared scallops on the nightly special were fantastic but the dish's sauce was a little light on flavor. -The prawn and ravioli special was excellent -The chicken Caesar was just okay -The shrimp pasta Alfredo was rich and hearty -The wine: we ordered the 3rd least expensive Chianti on the list (about $30) and it was not very good-I will never understand why restaurants put poor quality wines on their lists just to satisfy a price point. -The deserts (Tiramisu, Chocolate Gelato and chocolate cake) were all excellent, but the coffee was weak and dishwater-esque. Price: A little pricey for what you get. Overall we decided it was good enough to return, but I'm not itching to get back.
label: NEG

text: Yes, Ben & Jerry's is a chain. Yes, you can just buy the darn ice cream in a store. I don't care -- the Loop location is just plain fun to visit. As others have said, the workers here are really friendly -- even more friendly than other B&J locations. They honestly seem happy to have you in the store and are excited for you to taste their wares. Can't make up your mind? No problem! They'll give you as many samples as it takes for you to decide (provided you're legitimately going to buy things, of course. Don't abuse the generosity). Moreover, they don't do that weird singing/rhyming thing that other ice cream chains (down the street, ahem) do to "keep people happy." I'm happy enough with B&J's honesty and smiles, thanks. Ben & Jerry's has about 16-20 flavors available. There's plenty to offer everyone with tastes leaning toward chocolate, nuts, caramel or fruit. And while Ben & Jerry's is a chain, the workers (many are area university students) take pride in the store and really make it feel like a local hangout. Ben & Jerry's annual Free Cone Day happened last week. Any free food day has the potential to go from a great idea to a catastrophe in an hour (see Denny's, KFC, etc.). However, this B&J planned properly for the crowds and had plenty of ice cream left even when I arrived at 7 p.m. (some flavors were already out, it's true). The good vibes from the workers were transferred to the customer crowd, as there was no pushing, impatience or general negativity. Everyone really handled the day well.

text: I was in town and stayed at the Ambassador, which is right down the street from Mothers. I had been told, "Try the poboys at Mothers. They're the best." So I thought myself lucky that Mothers ended up being right down the street. Sadly, like the Cafe du Monde, Brennans, and the whole rest of my visit to New Orleans, Mothers was a serious let down. It's fried seafood on bread. That's it. There's no magic to it. There's gravy. There's also coleslaw of some sort (at least I think it was a vegetable). But there's no magic. Poboys are fried seafood sandwiches without a single thing to recommend them beyond saying "I tried one". The poor, unsuspecting seafood is mercilessly fried into submission. There's no taste to it beyond "crunch" and "grease". The bread, which is supposed to be unique to the poboy, tasted like generic crusty baguette. I feel I've had McFish sandwiches that tasted better than these did. Between the terrible food, the atrocious customer service, and the generally unappealing nature of the place, I can't find a single redeeming thing about the place. I know there are many people who rave about Mothers and the food in New Orleans. I guess it's just not to my taste.

text: Sending someone to eat here if they're looking for Vietnamese food is like telling someone to go a can of Chef Boyardee if they're looking for some Italian food. You just tell them that Vietnamese food doesn't exist in Santa Barbara and if it did, Saigon Noodle House is the armpit of that so-called Vietnamese food. Even if I wasn't a Viet from San Jose, it doesn't take one to realize that this place doesn't serve much better pho than the instant kind. Despite numerous owners over the year, the only thing that has changed is the place getting cleaner and the food alternating between crappy and really crappy. The pho lacks the beefy flavor and herbal notes, with extra MSG to compensate and the noodles are always overcooked. The meat is lacking and consistently past its sell by date. As for the bun thit nuong, the vermicelli is starchy and overdone, and what they consider the grilled pork seems to be a mesh of undercooked pork lacking any sort of seasoning. The thai iced tea has little tea and lots of milk, while the Vietnamese iced coffee (ca phe sua da) is weak and obviously brewed hours earlier. Santa Barbara may be lacking in Asian restaurants as a whole, but Saigon Noodle House takes it to a new low.

text: Who is this woman, Marsha Brown? We don't know, but she is spoken of by her staff as if she is an institution. She is a mystery, that Marsha, and her food is DAMN good. I went into this experience a bit apprehensive, as my girlfriend lives in New Orleans, I spend a great deal of time there, and we are both well acquainted with New Orleans cuisine. She was hesitant to go, but I was dying to get a taste of NOLA food up here. Let me put it this way: we stopped in on a Saturday for lunch and before we left, had already made our reservation for Sunday dinner. First, the building. It's an old church. How does one even acquire an old church? We don't know, but Marsha did it. I was a bit disappointed that we couldn't sit in the big church part for lunch, as they only had the bar area and the downstairs tables open. But it didn't matter. We had a fantastic and attentive bartender with whom we BS'd the entire time. And the food! Oh, the food. I had a "New Orleans style Philly cheesesteak" and it was better than any cheesesteak or po'boy I've ever eaten. The bread was perfect, the roast beef delicious, and it was covered in provolone cheese and Louisiana hot sauce. It may sound weird, but together it created the perfect sandwich. The fries were seasoned with something akin to Tony Cachere's, or perhaps a variety of Tony's. My girlfriend ordered the gumbo and actually liked it! The roux was very pretty and dark, and it was delicious. (Drinks: I had a key lime martini and was drunk about halfway through). Dinner the following night: it was quiet because it was late on a Sunday. Our reservation was for 9pm, and we were apparently the only people being seated at that time. We were led to the grandiose church, and there were only a few other diners there, all finishing up. We spent the majority of our dinner as the only two diners in a vast, beautiful church, with the attentive service all to ourselves. It was awesome. We decided to split some appetizers, some sides, and a single entree. First up: crawfish risotto. So delicious and creamy that I was scraping droppings off the tablecloth, and I declared that crawfish always tastes delicious because I associate it with fun. Then, a bacon slab. Literally, a really huge slab of bacon plated on some delicious sauce. Next up: we split a porckchop on a delicious corncake with sweet potato straw-like things, sweet potato casserole (identical to Ruth's Chris), and creamed spinach. It was all so delicious. We had to take a majority of it home, and didn't have room for dessert. Our personable and delightful server informed us that our choices would make "a beautiful dinner," and he was right. We had our food boxed up, but when I went to eat it, THE PORK CHOP WAS MISSING. I was so mad about that pork chop. I still am. Where did my pork chop go? I guess I'll never know. Hmmph. I'll guess I'll have to be going back to Marsha's to get another.
label: POS

text: I enjoy good local brews, and when I heard that Upland opened a tasting room in Broad Ripple I had to stop by. I took a beer fanatic friend with me, and we ordered a tasting of 8 beers (all on tap). Now, I've never had an "authentic" beer tasting experience. I've sampled beer at festivals, and went to a lot of wine tastings, and both experiences are dramatically diffferent. My experience at Upland was disappointing and unimpressive in the least. The woman serving us had to ask for help from other staff because she wasn't versed in the beer, and without even tasting the beer they tried to sell us growlers. We sat down on a vintage couch and she brought our beer tasting over to us, explaining to us the layout and that it followed the beer menu. I grabbed the beer menu at our table and she said "Oh no, that is outdated, we need to update that, we don't have most of those" and then pointed at the chalkboard that was a good 20 feet or so away from us. We had to attempt to read the chalkboard as we sampled our beers, and instead of removing the incorrect menus, she just left it on the table. All of the beers we drank were unimpressed. I like pils, browns and reds - they only had a pilsener and Miller Lite had a more full flavored taste. The other beers were unsatisfying, and my friend, who travels nationwide for good beer, was unimpressed and disappointed by the assortment. The worst beer was a "smoked" beer, which tasted like it was skunked. As we were drinking our samples (which he drank them all basically, not wanting to waste) the staff didn't check on any of the tables, they hung out behind the counter, and then proceeded to put fish in their tv fish tank. The woman who waited on us was bent over next to my friend, putting the fish in the fish tank, and her pants were scooting down her butt - she had no underwear on!! Here she was, with her butt crack hanging out, serving beer. Sure sure - people go commando all the time - but, to see it up close and personal (two feet away) while we're drinking our mediocre to bad beers, was gross. Real sanitary. I went up to the counter, paid for the beer, and she didn't ask if I wanted a growler this time, but, we thanked them and left. The decor is rather coffeehouse like, with vintage book shelves, bright colors...very...Bloomington. There are only certain days when you can order pints, and they do have growler specials on certain days. Overall a really dissatisfying experience, and I'm not sure if I'll ever go back. I have a feeling the other reviews here will be more positive, but, I'll take Sunking and Barley Island anytime.
label: NEG

text: City Park is the most beautiful place in New Orleans and is one of my favorite places in the WORLD. When I'm in the area I always drive through the park plus we go there as often as we can to play on the swings, look at the ducks and swans, and walk around. Storyland has been renovated (in fact they are still working on it) and it looks better than I remember in 35 years. It is the best place to take kids where they can walk inside of Pinnochio's whale, climb Ole King Cole's castle and "ride" inside Cinderella's pumpkin carriage. The amusement park has the carousel and the ladybug roller coaster that is perfect for 5 year old thrill seekers. You also have to take the train around the park and then check out the little miniature train garden that is a model of New Orleans made from bark, moss, leaves, etc. The best time to go is- anytime, but of course when the weather is nice and for Celebration in the Oaks when the whole thing is lit up and there is music and Christmas trees and Yuletide fun (and a cheesy but fun presentation of the Cajun Night Before Christmas in lights.) Also, this is the perfect place to have a wedding (we did, in the rose garden.) There is a large pavillion now for weddings and receptions and it is so elegant (and you don't have to dance on bricks.)

text: Again, another groupon purchase for me. I met my husband here for lunch one day, and it was pretty disappointing. Don't get me wrong, I love fresh ingredients, but it really doesn't do anything for the soup. It just seemed like a cheap way to bulk up a tiny $3 cup of soup. Both the rolls were pretty bland. The fish and avocado on the rainbow roll was flavorless (but then again, it was November in a landlocked state, so that probably expected). The El Camino roll, despite the ingredients, lacked flavor too. I was expecting a lot since it had cilantro, peppers, and lime juice, but it was truly lackluster. Also, it had a "sprinkling" of sesame oil on it, and the sesame oil tasted old. (My husband thought I was nuts when I said this, but sesame oil ages quickly. If you ever cook with it, you can identify this.) And the service? Slow. Very, very slow. It took an insane amount of time to get two bowls of soup and two rolls (that required no cooking). text: Well, I've ridden the system here for more than ten years, and I have to say, it's bad, but it's not quite horrible. The building here has a small museum, interesting for the kids. Mostly administrative and a few places to get coffee or sit down in. Yes, certain lines are overcrowded, it can be dangerous depending on which line you're on, there's always construction, and timing can be very horrendous. The regional rail lines usually have the best of it, with plenty of service, a mix of several trains and while sometimes delayed, most stations have the clocks up that tell you about how long you'll be waiting (or will announce delays). The trolley/subways are a bit dirty, although they did replace many of the cars on the blue line this decade, and it's a simple, relatively smooth system. The trolleys themselves are dangerous to pedestrians and other traffic, but all people need to be more aware of their surroundings, too. The bus system varies - Center City service is generally pretty smooth, but as you get outwards into the areas of the city beyond the little rectangle of Center City, the service drops downwards... suburbia is serviced by a few lines, like any other large metropolis, split into zones and while payment can be a bit confusing, it's not horrible. I still think the entire system could do without tokens, though. It's time to go the plastic card route of the MTA or almost any other system. They already do it for monthly passes. Stop taking money at all at the tellers and just adjust the machines to accept change. Make sure stops have a working method to enter the transport, too. And while the underground walking corridor is nice from 15th to 11th, clean it out frequently (power wash the corridor with a lot of water is my suggestion), and keep a patrol or two around each side, it scares some people (although you can just as easily walk above ground).

We usually start with one or two appetizers. Yangming's spring rolls, crab purses and dumplings are all nicely done. I've had their fillet, most of their chicken dishes and a tofu dish and each one was excellent. Always a special occasion, always gracious service, always lovely surroundings, this restaurant seems like a well-oiled, if slightly dated, machine. Highly recommended.

They have a drink called the "Goody" that is quite sweet but if you like that sort of thing give it a try. Go just for the experience and stay if you like the atmosphere!

text: Mmmm. The Old Spaghetti Factory is nothing special, so don't go if you are looking for gourmet Italian. I love the decor at OSF. It feels really cozy with warm colors, and if you are lucky you will get to sit inside of the traincar or right next to it some of their plush Queen Anne's style chairs - those chairs are the best! Tommy O is right - the Mizithra Cheese & Browned Butter Spaghetti is delish! I order the Italian Meatloaf and it comes with a nice portion of that on the side. The best thing about OSF is that every meal comes with your choice of iced tea or coffee, salad, bread and either spumoni or vanilla ice cream. Since the most expensive meal is around $13, this is a steal in downtown dining! If you go on a weekend though, be forewarned - you're going to wait for a long time during peak hours!

text: Well, we were heading down to the LA area for the weekend so the SO and I decided to go down 101 instead of our usual boring I-5 route. After watching a review from Cat Cora (from the food network) about Cold Spring Tavern we decided to stop in Santa Barbara for lunch. My GPS warned me that we would be going on some "unverified roads" and that always means an area off the beaten path. Off 101 we climb up a stretch of road and head into the Los Padres National Forrest and start to wonder "what did we get ourselves into?" We come upon a very charming shack (and I mean that in the nicest way!) come to find out it was a stage coach stop back in the day and not much has been done since. We put our name in and enjoy a short wait outside enjoying the beautiful surroundings. Once inside, I ordered the lunch special which was a BBQ sandwich and the SO ordered the French Dip. Both were delicious while the service was courteous and friendly. The meat was sliced thick and was very flavorful with a great smoke infused flavor along with a tangy BBQ sauce that wasn't over the top. The SO's french dip had nice slices of tri tip and came with an Au Jus with super flavor. All in all a great find and a fun place.

The spicy empanadas were so good I had a second order and my friends said their calamari was the best they'd ever had. The drinks on the menu were creative and fun, some contained cotton candy, and others with sugar sticks or topped with champagne. What it really comes down to for me is the service. Many bartenders in the city are jaded or just miserable behind the bar, but these guys were great!! The bartender/bar manager was so knowledgeable he even took the time to explain the difference between Tempranillo and Malbec to me which I found intruiging. Not that I speak of lick of Spanish, but just having that on brings me right back to California. The tacos are fresh and filled with delicious flavorful ingredients. The service was awesome too, everyone was very nice and quick to serve you and move the line along. The place is not huge, but what good Taqueria is, I ask you? The horchata was decent, but I have had better, sometimes it is better than others so if you want to take a chance and you are feeling bold, I say hey, why not. I understand where the owner's coming from, and he's told me about how difficult the move has been on him financially while also being more convenient for him, but I think he went in over his head and has really screwed over his customers as a result.

text: I am a member of a profound and prodigious club called the B.E.C., or Big Eaters Club. There are two ways to gain entry into our debauched society. The first is to go out with three established members of the B.E.C. to a restaurant with an approved, sizable menu, and with the group, order and devour all the restaurant has to offer. The second is to completely finish a Zaftig at the Famous Fourth Street Deli. The first option is easier. Ezekial F., one passionate member of the B.E.C., first introduced this behemoth of a sandwich to us by bringing an unfinished half of with a scale that dictated its weight: 1.6 pounds. Half. 1.6 pounds. Half. Fitting both slices of bread, with all that meat, between your teeth is akin to trying to fit a bowling ball inside a zip-lock bag. The corned beef is surprisingly tender, and generally falls apart with the slightest application of force. This is particularly important, because towards the end of your meal, if you make it that far, your jaws lack the energy and strength to chew. The one thing that keeps you going is the high quality of all the ingredients. The most die-hard of B.E.Cers will follow this monstrosity with dessert. Each slice of Checkerboard Cake is as big War and Peace in 14 font. And the eclairs are as big as my Danskos. My wife, the founding member of the B.D.E.C. (D for dessert) will split the two of them with me. The ensuing walk home is spent in a unique balance of comatose, pain and pride. And then we don't eat for three days.

text: Now, I'm very easy to please. There are very few times where I'm not willing to come back and give you another try. But unfortunately, Tasty Asia is not one of those places. text: Following rave reviews by Edmonton news, media, and internet blogs, it was decided that The Blue Pear would be the next restaurant splurge. I mean, having been called either the best or second best restaurant in Edmonton, no price can be too large right? So reservations were made for Sunday to take advantage of the Baby Pear special for a $59 three course dinner. First impressions: the front door is locked! Don't worry, they're not closed, you just need to ring the doorbell to enter. We were seated in the small dining room consisting of about 8-10 tables. Nice and cozy right? wrong. Tables were spaced too close, and the live sax and piano playing that night made it impossible to have a conversation. It was always a relief when the musicians took their coffee break. We were met by who we assumed to be the owner, a surly middle aged woman with a natural scowl. When we said we would be fine with water, we were replied with "would that be just tap water?" No, we would like Don Perrier with "just tap water" ice. Anyways, on to the food Bread: Completely boring and disappointing. Slices of white and brown bread that looks and tastes of any department store bread. Compared to say, Wildflower's in-house baked brioche and choice of goat's or cow's butter, base lead vs. sublime gold? Appetizers: Corn chowder - with popcorn and white truffle oil. Probably the best dish of the night. Fragrant corn flavour, with bits of fresh corn and smokey toasty popcorn, accented well with a hint of truffle. Salad - classic combo with serrano ham, canteloupe, arugula, and what they called a balsamic "glee", basically 3 drops of balsamic on an uninspired salad Entree: Beef three ways - Certainly a sad and boring plate if I've ever seen one. Three pieces of brown with a brown sauce. Braised beef cheeks, grilled tenderloin, and oxtail-potato terrine type square. All covered in a reduced red-wine sauce, all tasted exactly the same. To accompany the beef, brown and mushy green tomatoes with a marrow crumble, heavy and sludgy, the opposite of what you want to be paired with such a leaden dish. One of the worst dishes I've had, from any restaurant. Different textures of brown is what it should have been called as everything tasted pretty much the same. Duck - Cherry wood smoked duck confit, seared duck breast, cabbage hash with poached egg, with local sour cherry and mustard jam, accompanied with a foie gras biscuit. All four elements isolated in a lonely corner on a square plate. Duck breast was nicely seared and paired well with a tart cherry sauce. Duck confit so salty it was inedible, your kidneys will wince with every bite. Cabbage hash with poached egg was flavourful but lacked connection with the rest of the dish. Dessert: Creme brulee - Well it wasn't creme brulee, it was more like gelatinized cream with a carmelized sugar circle placed on top, if you could have rubberized vanilla for dessert this was it. First of all, how is it possible to turn a creme brulee out of its ramekin and have it still standing perfectly upright? shame on you. Might have just called it vanilla jello. Flourless chocolate cake - Tasty and rich chocolate goodness with orange liqueur and orange sorbet. Simple and good. Orange and chocolate, can't go wrong with that. Conclusion: Overly pretentious, pompous, and poorly thought out dishes made for an evening that certainly begged for more. It wasn't so much that the food wasn't worth it, it was just plain bad. It wasn't the price but the overall quality and execution of the food that was poor. Espeically with a price tag of over $120 for a dinner for two, you won't see me ringing The Blue Pear's doorbell again. Compared to my meal at Wildflower Grill, where you could tell they put emphasis on satisfying the customer and ensuring that felt appreciated, every dish thoughtfully planned and constructed, the Blue Pear fell far behind in every aspect.

text: If I was given the opportunity to steal a few US art museums, The Walters Museum in Baltimore would be on my short list. When I lived on the east coast, I visited The Walters regularly. It's a great museum located in a truly picturesque center of historic Baltimore. That's why I was glad to visit the Santa Barbara Museum of Art for their exhibition, Delacroix to Monet: Masterpieces of 19th-Century Painting from the Walters Art Museum. I remembered a few old favorites but one painting, by an artist with whom I was not familiar, riveted me: a small 5x7 oil on panel titled 'An Ecclesiastic', circa 1874, by painter Mariano José María Bernardo Fortuny y Carbó. An elderly gentleman -- whose puffy, tired face is painted in daubs of grey, pink and green -- sits on a chair barely visible beneath his pink-hued robes that cascade over his rotund body. The solitary figure, surrounded by a solid blood-orange background, stares intently at the viewer. This one painting is like no other in the exhibition and, as the description on the wall mentions, the similarity to works by Francis Bacon cannot be ignored. The composition reminded me of the painting popularly known as 'Whistler's Mother', painted only three years earlier, of a woman in long black robes against an almost solid color background. (Bernardo's work is, by comparison, gratuitously cropped on all sides to enhance its immediacy.) It was the stare of Bernardo's subject that called to mind the modern portraits by Mexican painter, Rafael Coronel, too, as the haunting gaze of this man centered in the sea of a bright solid background drew me back to this painting at least six times before I left the museum.

It's really something to watch, and you can taste the moist freshness with each bite. The shaved are also good, albeit thicker and plumper (think shawarma shaved meat in size and shape). 2). Prices are CHEAP! They must make enough of a profit margin to continue as this price point, and I'm glad for it. These dishes are some of the least pricey in Chinatown, comparatively speaking. Tonight I stuffed myself for $7.15 with tip included. 3). They don't waste time here. If you're by yourself, you can sit with other people at a communal table. The waitresses take your order quickly and deliver the food fast. There is high turnover. So don't be insulted if your check is dropped before you're finished. All in all, Nanzhou Hand Drawn Noodle House is a real winner. Bring a friend.

text: The quest for the great Philly Xiolóngbao, also known as soup dumpling, or my night out with my buddy Jim: First off, let me say that my friend Jim and I were poised for a huge let-down from this quest's first conception. In fact, he christened it the GXLBD2010 - or, the Great XiaoLongBao Disappointment of 2010. Our quest was to seek the soup dumpling in Philadelphia's China Town and to find a specimen worthy of our affection and loyalty. We had low expectations as he had previously dabbled in the dark arts of Philly soup dumpling quests and we both felt like we had already had the best soup dumpling on offer in the region in Flushing, Queens at a magic spot known as Nan Xiang where the soup dumplings are made by the hands of angels (http://newyork.seriouseats.com/2009/02/best-soup-dumplings-nan-xiang-xiao-long-bao-flushing-nyc.html). There had been some recent buzz around town, though, that Philly was now home to some spots offering some perfectly fine soup dumplings, so with doubt in our hearts and the memory of Nan Xiang driving us to find soup dumplings closer to home - we set out. It is important to explain what, in our opinion, a soup dumpling should be. It should be a delicate little bag of soup compromised of savory pork (or pork and crab - depending on which kind you order), which is all swimming in delicious broth encased in a delicate dumpling wrapper. The skin of the dumpling should not be too thick, but should be tough enough to contain the soup and meat. The meat to soup ratio is important as you don't want a dumpling that is dry, nor do you want just broth and no meat. The key is balance and you know when it is right. We decided that we would sample every pork soup dumpling we knew to be on offer in China town. We girded ourselves with a cocktail and set off to our first destination: Dim Sum Garden. We ordered the pork soup dumplings and a cucumber salad. The place itself is more cheery inside than one might expect given its location under the Market East "overpass" next to a bus depot. The décor was bright; all was clean and inviting. The tea was good, which we took as a positive omen of things to come. However, when the dumplings arrived, the wrappers were gummy and the insides had a bland pork meatball, not much broth, and some liquefied pork fat that we dubbed "meat goo." We decided that these soup dumplings were not horrible, but nothing in comparison to those on offer in Flushing. In addition, the cucumber salad had seeds in it and the salad was over-dressed in sesame oil and soy sauce. The pieces were unevenly chopped too, which is something that does not affect flavor but does belie the care that the kitchen takes with its ingredients. On a 1-10 scale - these dumplings got a score of 4. See my review of Sang Kee (http://www.yelp.com/biz/sang-kee-peking-duck-house-philadelphia-2#hrid:6clxlgVLTR-HljLTZUeeag) - our second stop. See my review for Sakura (http://www.yelp.com/bi...), which won by the way, for our last stop.

I asked that my food be prepared extra spicy and don't put sugar in any of the dishes. Secret: sugar is added to "Americanize the dish" Appetizer: Fried large shrimp in 3 flavor dip. The sight of the dishes made me wanted to walk out but since my friend picked this restaurant, I thought it best that I stayed. I asked for Thai hot sauce and not the bottle of Viet hot sauce I saw and the waitress offers Sirachi to me anyway. She came back to the table with vinegar with peppers in it. Hmmm, the last time I checked, Thai hot sauce was exactly that, Thai hot sauce. All 3 dishes were awful. I can't even describe the texture of the fish but I don't recommend you ordering this. The chicken was not tender at all probably bcz it was overcooked. I looked for the crawfish but only found these little undeveined shrimp...yuk! For an appetizer, 3 main course, and a bottle of Tsing Tao (Chinese beer), the check came to $57.80. I would have been happier at a fast food place. Authentic? NOT Would I ever eat here again? Not even for free Too bad I couldn't have cooked my own food!

text: I visited Bridge last week as part of a tweetup and for dinner with out-of-town guests. The location was perfect for our transit tweetup, as Bridge is just a few blocks from the 8th and Pine Metrolink station downtown and just near Left Bank Books (easy to reach everything in downtown, really). It's also just two blocks from my loft, so I'll likely be visiting regularly. The tweetup folks had secured Bridge's main level for finger foods and mingling. It was a little tight, as it's a narrow space, but it suited our group just fine. I love the wall-tall windows looking out to the street, and the bar is large and beautiful. Another super-awesome thing? Bridge is completely smoke-free! My friends and I needed something a bit more substantial for dinner than just cheese appetizers, though, so we moved upstairs to order entrees. As others have mentioned, Bridge's upper level is a little warmer than the lower level (heat rises, after all), but I didn't mind it, as it wasn't overly hot. Upstairs, tables are covered and candles are lit. It's inviting and cozy. More: there was a half-wall/ledge thing that was next to our table, so we had a place to put purses and laptop bags. Handy! Bridge is smart and leaves a carafe of water on the table so you don't have to flag down a server every 8 minutes -- being a fast water drinker, I love this. Bridge's menu is phenomenal. Our group shared an appetizer of peppered goat cheese, foccacia, olives, hazelnuts and roasted tomatoes. We all had have our weird food quirks, but among us, we devoured everything except a few olives. The bread was slightly crispy outside and spongy inside, and it went perfectly with the goat cheese. For my dinner, I ordered an "adult" grilled cheese sandwich -- different cheeses, onion and tomato on a roasted bun. I'm all about cheese, and this sandwich certainly hit the spot. I was starting to fill up after the great cheese board appetizer, so I only ate half of my sandwich. The other half held up well when I reheated it the next day. My sandwich came with potato chips from St. Louis' own Billy Goat Chip Company. SO crispy, seasoned and delicious! (There were options for other sides, but I don't remember what they were) I also had a side of a bean salad in a vinegar dressing. It was yummy. A friend had ordered a pot of mac and cheese. VERY cheesy, and the sauce had some finely chopped tomatoes in it. I stole a bite, and I'd totally order it next time. The only things I wasn't in love with at Bridge were the low lighting and the loudness. I found myself tilting the menu closer to the candle to get just a bit more light to read everything. And the sound from the tweetup on the lower level carried upstairs (the upstairs overlooks the downstairs instead of being a full, separate floor). I don't know if the sound issues were just from this event or if it's always like that. But it became increasingly difficult to chat at our table. I do wish Bridge would post menu items on its website as HTML instead of PDF, as that's annoying, particularly when browsing on a phone. My sandwich/chips entree was about $8 and the cheese board was about $12 -- fair prices for the deliciousness that was consumed. I'd go back to Bridge. There were plenty of enticing dishes that caught my eye. Bridge has enough vegetarian and meaty entrees and appetizers for everyone.

Selling only a few pies at first, they have now expanded to selling around 100 pies per Sunday between 5pm and 2am. They take orders until the dough runs out and you had better call in early because they always sell out!! The pizzas are very good! The crust is perfect. The cheese is not greasy. And the red sauce is simply amazing. The ingredients are all very fresh and tasty. And all this non-greasy flavor doesn't cost you much at all...an 18" pizza is only around $15. You really cannot go wrong here. They only make good food! The shop itself is extremely eclectic. You simply walk down a short alleyway and exchange cash only for your order. The people running the place have a very cool vibe and just seem to be having fun with their little side business. I would rate this the best pizza in Nola.

text: Had dinner here tonight with a friend who just moved into the neighborhood. There was a line out the door at Hook's across the street, but it turns out this place is better -- at least for sushi. The sign above the front door, which reads "the art of Asian cuisine" hints at the creativity of Sushi Rock's makizushi. For example, the Lollipop Roll (salmon and crab) comes wrapped in a thinly peeled cucumber rather than a traditional seaweed nori, and its fresh, clean texture is complemented nicely by a tart ponzu sauce. Another inventive item is the Sushi Rock Tuna (tuna, crab, asparagus), a rice-free roll that's lightly battered and tempura-fried in a pair of sauces. Speaking of sauces, they're a big part of what makes Sushi Rock's feel unique -- from the pineapple sauce on the Hawaiian to the spicy aioli on the grouper to the "dynamite action-packed cream sauce" on the 007. Everything we tried was fresh and flavorful, and the service was friendly and professional. Our only minor quibbles are that the place is REALLY dark -- I could barely read the menu -- and they were out of conch, but happily subbed in crab on our Island Volcano Roll. The only thing we tried from the regular dinner menu was a traditional gyoza appetizer, which was fine but not extraordinary. Nitpicking aside, I'll definitely be back. (2/4/2009)

I would've much rather waited 10 minutes to have my nails done at one of their many manicure stations. Then what was ridiculous is that I had nail polish all over my fingers. I am horrible at painting my own nails, but I could have done a better job myself. text: Gosh, what a disappointment. I travel to Santa Barbara quite frequently for work (and ok, a little bit of pleasure while I'm at it) and tend to stay in this neighborhood every time. I didn't want it and when I told the front desk agent that, he tried to scare me out of parking on the street. In addition, every other hotel I've stayed at in the area has provided free parking... just sayin. Walking to my room, I was excited about my stay as I passed by several cute looking rooms. text: The smartest new bar in Philadelphia, I was worried if they'd survive or not. Thankfully Philly is indeed ready for this fantastic concept which continues to improve with every visit. Standing among the hundreds of bottles of spirits, elixirs, tinctures, essences, extracts, and substances are some of the most talented, informed mixologists I have ever had the pleasure to meet. The vibe is, for me, slightly more reminiscent of a mortuary versus an apothecary, but hey, you Goths should love it. Easy with the metal stools though people, they are not bongos and yes, we're pissed at the huge noise you just made knocking your stool over. I've had both the best drink I've ever had here (a recent concoction that was a mix of margarita, sage, and soy sauce plus other 'secret' ingredients), and the worst (my own doing, so I'll not saddle you with that tale, let me just say to listen to your bartender). Note that other than that one drink, everything else I have had has been spectacular. I miss the Three Sheiks, though (maybe it was Two Sheiks, but by the end of the night I was seeing three) regardless, bring it back guys, it was delish. The food is just as sumptuous as the drinks are, and I'm a huge fan of tapas so the ability to get a bunch of plates as we sample cocktails through the evening just makes the place that much better. So indulge your experimental side and climb above the standard fare you're used to. Enjoy food and drink that excites your mind as well as your palate. And please, don't play with your stool.
